# Interruption recovery

The committed work-item log is the durable record at stage boundaries. The ignored
`.delivery/interruption-checkpoint.json` is the write-ahead recovery record inside one working tree. It
does not replace a work item, a commit, or a handoff. It lets a person stop one coding agent and open the
same working tree with another without requiring either agent to contact the other.

## Recover before starting work

Run this before starting or selecting a card:

    python3 .delivery/checkpoint.py status

If it reports `active` or `abandoned`, do not start another card and do not assume the saved `next` action
already happened. Read the named work item and its latest log entries, then inspect `git status`,
`git diff`, `git log --oneline --graph --all`, and the checkpoint's saved-versus-current Git snapshots.
Classify every current change as completed, incomplete, or unrelated. Stop for unrelated work. Once the
recovery action is supported by the files, adopt the checkpoint:

    python3 .delivery/checkpoint.py resume --next "<exact next action>"

A read-only stage can be rerun from its inputs when interrupted. Its orchestrator owns the checkpoint.

## Start before the stage

Before the first stage action, create the write-ahead record:

    python3 .delivery/checkpoint.py start \
      --card "<card-id or unassigned request>" \
      --stage "<stage>" \
      --objective "<one observable stage outcome>" \
      --next "<first exact action>" \
      [--candidate "<full commit id or not-yet-built>"]

`start` refuses to replace active work. The checkpoint requires the project's Git working-tree root.

## Update while working

Checkpoint at every coherent unit of work and immediately before a long-running or state-changing action.
The `--next` value states what has not happened yet. Add only facts observed in this session:

    python3 .delivery/checkpoint.py update \
      [--completed "<durable edit or decision now visible in the files>"] \
      [--check "<command and observed exit status or result>"] \
      [--candidate "<full commit id or not-yet-built>"] \
      --next "<exact next action>"

Before running a long command, update `--next` to that command. After it returns, record the observed result
and replace `--next`. This write-ahead order bounds lost context to the action in flight. Never put secrets,
personal data, exploit details, credentials, or command arguments containing them in the checkpoint.

## Finish only after durable handoff

First append the stage result to the work-item log, commit the stage artifacts and evidence as the
orchestrator requires, and verify the tree is clean. Obtain the full evidence-commit ID with
`git rev-parse HEAD`, then run:

    python3 .delivery/checkpoint.py finish --evidence "<full evidence-commit id>"

`finish` refuses a dirty tree, a shortened or nonexistent commit, and a commit that is not an ancestor of
`HEAD`. A finished checkpoint is quiet at later session starts and may be replaced by the next stage.

Only a person may decide to discard in-progress work. On that explicit instruction, retain the recovery
record with:

    python3 .delivery/checkpoint.py abandon --reason "<person's reason>"

Abandoning does not clean or delete files. A later session may resume the retained checkpoint.

## Scope and guarantees

Writes use a temporary file, file flush, atomic replace, and directory flush where the platform supports
it. A process killed during a write leaves either the prior valid checkpoint or the new one. The session
start/resume hook reports unfinished checkpoints automatically.

The checkpoint is ignored by Git because it can describe uncommitted work. It follows the working tree,
not a clone or another machine. To move work elsewhere, first create the normal clean, committed handoff.
